hook_text: You've been using half of the cosine rule since grade 8. The other half is just a corner with attitude.
clip_script: Two friends leave the same gate. One walks seven metres, the other eight. How far apart are they? Everyone shouts Pythagoras — square, add, root: about ten comma six. But that only works if the corner between their paths is EXACTLY ninety degrees. Real corners have attitude. Enter the cosine rule: a squared equals b squared plus c squared — that's literally Pythagoras — MINUS two b c cos of the corner. That last term is the attitude adjustment. Corner tighter than ninety? Cosine is positive, the correction subtracts, the friends end up CLOSER. Corner wider than ninety — say a hundred and twenty degrees? Cosine goes NEGATIVE. Minus times minus is plus: one hundred and thirteen plus fifty-six is one hundred and sixty-nine. Square root: thirteen metres. Wider corner, further apart — the formula literally knows geometry. And at exactly ninety? Cos of ninety is zero, the adjustment vanishes, and Pythagoras walks out of the jacket. That's the whole rule: Pythagoras, plus a term that measures how far your corner leans from square. Wide corner but your answer got SHORTER? You dropped a minus. The geometry just caught your calculator error.
visual_style: Two glowing paths swing open and closed at an animated corner like a door hinge; the correction term pulses red and green as the angle crosses ninety, and the distance readout stretches and shrinks live with the corner.
pacing: Fast setup, hinge-swinging demonstration, dramatic sign flip at ninety degrees, clean 13-metre payoff.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and give every corner its attitude adjustment.
